Subject: The Morning Market Call - Thursday September 6th, 2001.

Good morning,

Stocks head into Thursday on shaky footing after yesterday's session, as a fresh round of earnings warnings kept technology shares under pressure and investors stayed cautious about the economic outlook. Futures are pointing to a soft open.

What we are watching today:

- Weekly jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. Another rise would reinforce fears about the labor market.
- The revised second-quarter productivity numbers.
- Comments from Fed officials following the Beige Book, which described a slow economy.
- Treasury yields, which have drifted lower as traders bet on further rate cuts.

With Friday's employment report on deck, expect volume to stay light and moves to be driven by headlines. We'd stay selective and keep an eye on risk.

More at midday.

Regards,
The Trading Desk

Subject: Concern about EBS

Hi Marcus,

I wanted to reach out about the EBS volumes attached to our production instances. I've been reviewing last month's AWS bill, and I noticed a few things that I think deserve a closer look before they turn into bigger problems.

First, our storage costs have climbed about 28% over the past quarter, even though traffic hasn't grown anywhere near that much. When I dug into it, I found roughly forty volumes that aren't attached to any running instance. Some of them look like leftovers from the staging migration in the spring. Together they're costing us a few hundred dollars a month, and nobody seems to own them.

Second, many of our snapshots have no retention policy. We have snapshots going back more than two years, and some of them are of volumes that no longer exist. I'm not sure whether any of them are still needed for compliance or recovery, which is exactly why I'd like to confirm before anyone deletes anything.

Third, I'm a little worried about performance on the database volumes. We're still on gp2 for a few of them, and during last week's reporting jobs I saw latency spikes that lined up with burst credits running out. Moving to gp3 would probably fix that and cost less, but I don't want to make that change without coordinating a maintenance window.

Here's what I'd suggest:

1. Tag every volume with an owner and a purpose, and flag anything untagged for review.
2. Set up lifecycle policies for snapshots, with a default of 30 to 90 days unless there's a reason to keep them longer.
3. Plan a gp2 to gp3 migration for the database volumes, starting with the least critical.

I can put together a spreadsheet listing the orphaned volumes and old snapshots by the end of the week. If you could look it over and tell me which ones are safe to remove, that would help a lot.

Do you have time to talk this through on Thursday? Fifteen minutes should be enough to agree on next steps.

Thanks,
Priya

**Abstract**

Thin films of the tetragonal L1₀ phase of Mn-Ga are of considerable interest for spintronic applications because of their large perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and low saturation magnetization. In this work, we investigate how epitaxial strain influences the magnetic properties of ultrathin L1₀ Mn-Ga films grown on single-crystal substrates. Films with thicknesses ranging from a few to several tens of nanometers were prepared and characterized by X-ray diffraction and magnetometry. We observe a pronounced reduction of the uniaxial anisotropy as film thickness decreases, accompanied by a measurable change in the tetragonal distortion of the lattice. These findings indicate that strain relaxation and interfacial effects progressively suppress the anisotropy in the ultrathin regime. The results clarify the limits of Mn-Ga as a perpendicular magnetic layer at reduced thickness and provide guidance for the design of thin-film devices.

# Navy to Rotate 1,200 Sailors Through Three Carriers in a Single Deployment

NORFOLK, Va. — About 1,200 sailors will take part in an unusual "three-hull swap," serving aboard three different aircraft carriers during one tour of duty, the Navy said.

Under the plan, the crew members will move from one ship to the next, each of which is named after a U.S. president. The arrangement is meant to keep the sailors together as a unit while the ships they operate change around them.

The journey will begin in Japan, where the sailors will start their tour. From there, they will travel around South America to Virginia, where they will take over a second carrier. The crew will then head back west, crossing toward the Pacific, to reach San Diego, where the third hull awaits.

Navy officials have described the swap as a way to make efficient use of experienced personnel as ships move between homeports and maintenance schedules. Rather than disbanding a team and rebuilding it, the Navy keeps a trained group of sailors in place and shifts the ships around them. Such a plan avoids the cost and disruption of moving a full crew each time a vessel changes location.

For the sailors, the experience will be unlike a typical deployment. Most spend a tour on one ship, learning its quirks, its layout and its routines. In this case, they will need to adapt to three vessels, each with its own particular characteristics, even if the carriers share a common design and mission.

The long voyage around South America is expected to be the most demanding part of the swap, covering thousands of miles. Carriers that make the trip are often visible reminders of the Navy's global reach, and the transit will include port visits and training along the way.

Families of the sailors will also feel the effects, as the changing locations may affect where they can meet loved ones and how long the sailors are away from home.

The Navy said the plan reflects broader efforts to manage a stretched fleet and to give crews continuity while ships are repaired, upgraded and redeployed.

Plenty of extras can change the flavor, texture and look of a loaf.

**Grains and seeds:** Sunflower, pumpkin, sesame, flax, poppy or chia seeds add crunch and nutrition. Rolled oats, cracked wheat or cooked quinoa give body.

**Flavor:** Herbs like rosemary, thyme or oregano work well, as do roasted garlic, caramelized onion, cheese, olives and sun-dried tomatoes. Black pepper or jalapeño add heat.

**Sweet additions:** Raisins, cranberries, chopped dates, walnuts, cinnamon, honey or molasses suit breakfast loaves.

**Texture and richness:** Milk, butter, olive oil, an egg or yogurt makes the crumb softer. Potato flakes or mashed potato keep bread moist.

**Other flours:** Rye, whole wheat or spelt add depth, and a spoonful of malt powder improves browning.

Fold in dry add-ins near the end of kneading so they distribute evenly.

The vault door was still swinging open when the first bullet struck Daniel Whitmore in the chest.

He had not intended to be shot. In truth, he had not intended to be robbing a bank at all, at least not until three weeks earlier, when the foreclosure notice arrived and the last of his savings vanished into a medical bill. The plan had been simple: a mask, a duffel bag, a toy-like pistol he had bought secondhand, and ten minutes of courage.

The security guard, a heavyset man named Ortiz, fired twice more. Daniel felt each impact as a hard push, as if someone had shoved him in a crowded corridor. He staggered back against a marble pillar. Then he looked down.

There were three holes in his jacket. There was no blood.

"Stay down!" Ortiz shouted, his voice cracking. He fired again. The round flattened against Daniel's shoulder and dropped to the floor with a small metallic sound.

For a moment the entire lobby went silent. The tellers, the customers lying on the tile, the guard with his smoking revolver: all of them stared at Daniel, and Daniel stared back.

"I think," he said slowly, "that something is wrong with the way this is working."

Ortiz lowered his weapon. His hands were trembling. "What are you?"

"I do not know," Daniel admitted. He removed the mask, because it seemed foolish to continue hiding. "I assure you, this is as much a surprise to me as it is to you."

Sirens approached in the distance. Daniel considered his position with the calm of a man who had just discovered that the rules had changed. He could flee with the money. He could, presumably, walk through the police line unharmed. Yet as he looked at the frightened faces on the floor, the thought of the duffel bag felt suddenly shameful.

He set it on the counter, unzipped and empty.

"I apologize for the disruption," he said to the nearest teller, a young woman clutching her badge. "I intended to take money. I will not be doing so."

Outside, the police had arrived in force. Daniel stepped into the sunlight with his hands raised. Officers shouted. Shots rang out, one after another, and each struck him and fell harmlessly away. He stood patiently until they stopped.

"Gentlemen," he said, "I am prepared to be arrested. I only ask that someone explain to me why I am unable to be harmed, because I would very much like to know."

A silence settled. Then the commanding officer, pale and unsure, slowly lowered his gun.

Daniel realized that being invincible did not solve his troubles. The foreclosure notice still waited at home. The medical bill had not shrunk. But something had altered. For the first time in months, he was not afraid, and he suspected that this change would matter more than any money in the vault.

He held out his wrists. "Please," he said. "Let us begin."

A helicopter autorotation is a way of landing safely after the engine fails or the tail rotor stops working. Instead of the engine driving the main rotor, the upward flow of air through the rotor, caused by the helicopter descending, keeps the blades turning. The pilot uses the stored energy in the spinning rotor to cushion the landing.

The principle is similar to a maple seed spinning as it falls. In normal flight, air is pulled down through the rotor disc. In autorotation, the helicopter descends, so air moves up through the disc and spins the blades. The rotor speed (RPM) has to be kept in a safe range, since too little means the blades lose lift and too much risks structural damage.

**Steps in a typical autorotation**

1. **Recognize the failure.** The pilot notices the warning horn or light, a change in engine noise, or a yaw of the nose as the torque disappears. Quick recognition is critical.

2. **Lower the collective immediately.** This reduces the pitch of the main rotor blades, which reduces drag and lets the rotor keep spinning. Doing this in about a second or two is vital, because the rotor will begin to slow down right away.

3. **Maintain rotor RPM.** The pilot checks the tachometer and adjusts the collective to keep RPM in the green arc.

4. **Establish the glide.** The pilot uses cyclic control to set the best glide speed, which differs by aircraft, often around 60 to 80 knots. Rotor RPM and airspeed are the two things to keep in check.

5. **Choose a landing area.** The pilot picks a suitable spot, ideally into the wind and clear of obstacles, and steers toward it. Pedals are used to keep the helicopter in trim.

6. **Make a radio call and prepare for landing.** If time allows, the pilot declares an emergency and does a quick check for the cause of the failure, such as an attempt to restart the engine.

7. **Flare.** At roughly 40 to 100 feet above the ground, the pilot pulls the cyclic back to raise the nose. This slows the forward speed and the rate of descent, and it also increases rotor RPM.

8. **Level the aircraft.** Just before touchdown, the pilot levels the helicopter with the cyclic so that it will land on its skids or wheels.

9. **Cushion the landing.** Near the ground, the pilot pulls up the collective to use the rotor's remaining energy, which slows the descent and softens the touchdown.

10. **Land and lower the collective.** After touchdown the pilot keeps the cyclic neutral, lowers the collective fully, and brings the aircraft to a stop.

Pilots practice autorotations regularly in training, often to a power recovery, so the maneuver becomes instinctive.

Mesons with spin-exotic quantum numbers, such as J^PC = 1^−+, cannot be formed from a quark-antiquark pair alone and are therefore regarded as clear signatures of hybrid mesons or multiquark states. The COMPASS experiment at CERN searches for such states in diffractive dissociation of a 190 GeV/c negative pion beam on a proton target, using the large acceptance of its two-stage magnetic spectrometer. We present new results of partial-wave analyses of the final states π−π−π+, ηπ− and η′π−, which were extracted from the same data sample. In all of these channels, a significant intensity is observed in the spin-exotic 1^−+ wave. The resonant nature of the signal is studied by fitting the mass dependence of the partial-wave amplitudes, including the phase motion relative to well-established resonances. The resulting parameters of the π1(1600) are compared across decay modes, and the role of non-resonant contributions in the 1^−+ wave is discussed.

Single-use plastics are everywhere in our daily lives. We use plastic bags, straws, bottles, and cutlery for a few minutes and then throw them away. However, these items do not disappear. I believe governments should ban single-use plastic products, because the harm they cause far outweighs their convenience.

The first reason is environmental damage. Plastic takes hundreds of years to break down. Meanwhile, it ends up in oceans, rivers, and landfills. Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed plastic fragments to their chicks. Over time, plastic breaks into tiny microplastics, which have now been found in drinking water, food, and even human blood. This is a threat to both wildlife and people.

Second, recycling alone is not enough. Many people believe that putting plastic in a recycling bin solves the problem, but only about nine percent of all plastic ever made has been recycled. Governments cannot depend on individuals to fix this problem when the system itself is flawed. A ban sends a clear message and pushes companies to find better solutions.

Some people argue that a ban would raise costs for businesses and consumers. This is a fair concern. However, many countries have already introduced bans, and they have managed the change successfully. Reusable bags, paper straws, and refillable containers are now common, and they often become cheaper as more people use them.

In conclusion, banning single-use plastics is a practical and necessary step. It protects the environment, encourages innovation, and shows that society takes its responsibility to future generations seriously.

The thread had four thousand upvotes by the time Karl Reinhardt finished reading it aloud to his grandfather, who sat in the corner of the Bremen apartment with a blanket over his knees, listening with his eyes closed.

"Read the top comment again," the old man said.

Karl cleared his throat. "'Imagine a Germany that was torn apart, occupied, and made to pay. Imagine a Europe divided between rival powers, with armies on every border. Imagine the Reich in ruins, and no Führer to guide it.' Opa, it's just a writing prompt. Everyone knows it's fantasy."

"Is it?"

"Obviously. The Allies lost. We won. The Reich is strong. Look around."

His grandfather opened his eyes. They were pale and watery, but they didn't waver. "I'm ninety-one years old, Karl. I have looked around for a very long time."

Karl wanted to laugh, but something in the old man's face stopped him. Outside, the evening broadcast was starting. Through the thin walls came the familiar anthem, the same one that had opened every evening of his life.

"In the story," Karl said slowly, "people write that the world would be free. That you could say what you liked. That no one would disappear in the night." He shrugged. "Nobody believes that. Nobody could."

"I had a brother," said his grandfather. "Matthias. He said something once, in 1943, in a bakery, and by morning he was gone. Your grandmother told me not to look for him. So I didn't." He paused. "I have never forgiven myself for obeying."

The room was quiet. The anthem swelled through the wall.

"You want to know what that world would be like?" the old man said. "I think it would be a world where you could ask me this question without lowering your voice."

Karl realized he had been whispering the entire time.

He looked at the screen, at the thousands of strangers imagining a world in which they were not afraid, and he felt something he had no name for, something that had been trained out of him before he could walk.

"Write something," his grandfather said. "Under their story. Just one line."

"They'd trace it."

"Probably."

Karl's fingers hovered over the keyboard. Down in the street a patrol car rolled past, slow and unhurried. He thought of Matthias and the bakery and the sound of a door closing.

Then, carefully, he typed: *I think I would have liked to live there.*

He did not press send. Not yet. But for the first time in his life, he left the words on the screen, and he did not delete them.

Cuteness is subjective, but some animals consistently top people's lists.

**Baby animals in general** tend to win, thanks to big eyes, round faces and clumsy movements. Puppies, kittens and ducklings all qualify.

Among wild species, a few stand out:

- **Red pandas** have fluffy russet fur, a ringed tail and a round, masked face.
- **Sea otters** hold hands while they sleep so they do not drift apart, and they float on their backs cracking shells on their bellies.
- **Quokkas**, small marsupials from Western Australia, appear to smile constantly.
- **Baby elephants** wobble around on thick legs and trip over their own trunks.
- **Fennec foxes** have enormous ears and tiny bodies.
- **Pygmy hedgehogs** curl into spiny balls that fit in your palm.
- **Axolotls**, with their feathery gills and permanent grin, have a devoted following.
- **Penguin chicks** are covered in fuzzy gray down and waddle awkwardly.

Scientists have a term for the reaction these animals cause, the "baby schema" effect, which describes how features like big eyes and rounded heads trigger our caring instincts.

Here are five ways to use a ripe avocado.

1. **Classic guacamole.** Mash the avocado with lime juice, salt, diced red onion, cilantro and a little chopped jalapeno. Keep some chunks for texture.

2. **Avocado toast.** Spread it on thick, crusty toast and finish with flaky salt, chili flakes and a squeeze of lemon. A fried or poached egg on top turns it into a full meal.

3. **Creamy smoothie.** Blend half an avocado with a banana, spinach, milk of your choice and a little honey. It adds a silky texture without a strong flavor.

4. **Chocolate mousse.** Blend avocado with cocoa powder, maple syrup, a splash of milk and a pinch of salt until completely smooth. Chill it for an hour. It is rich and surprisingly decadent.

5. **Stuffed avocado.** Halve it, remove the pit and fill the hollow with tuna salad, chicken salad, or a mix of tomato, corn and black beans. Eat it straight from the skin with a spoon.

**Abstract**

We present adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) simulations of the cosmological light cone, designed to produce synthetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZE) survey data. Using a hydrodynamic code with adaptive refinement, we follow the formation of galaxy clusters in a large cosmological volume and construct a light cone by stacking and projecting simulation outputs along the line of sight. Gas properties, including temperature and density, are used to compute the thermal SZE signal for each cluster. We obtain mock SZE maps, cluster catalogs, and the resulting number counts as a function of redshift and signal strength. These synthetic surveys allow us to test cluster-finding strategies and to quantify selection effects relevant to current and upcoming millimeter-wave experiments, and to assess how sensitive cluster counts are to the underlying cosmological parameters.

# Palmer Says He Understands Why Woods Is Staying Away From Bay Hill

**ORLANDO, Fla.** — Arnold Palmer says he does not hold it against Tiger Woods that the world's most famous golfer will not be teeing it up at the tournament that carries Palmer's name.

Palmer, the 85-year-old king of golf and host of the Arnold Palmer Invitational, said this week that he understands the reasoning behind Woods' decision to skip the event at Bay Hill. Woods has been a fixture there for most of his career and has won the tournament more times than any other player, but he has been dealing with a game that has not held together, and he is trying to use his time carefully.

"I know what he's going through," Palmer said. "A player has to do what he thinks is best for his game, and I respect that. I'd love to have him here, and the fans would too, but I understand."

Woods is struggling to be ready for next month's Masters at Augusta National, where he has won four green jackets. The question of whether he can sharpen his game in time has hung over his preparations for weeks. His recent appearances have been marked by errant tee shots, uncertain short-game play and a visible lack of rhythm, a stark contrast to the dominant form that carried him to 14 major championships.

For Woods, the calendar is working against him. With the Masters only weeks away, every day away from competition is a calculated risk. Players who miss tournaments before a major lose the chance to work through problems under pressure, but Woods and his team appear to have decided that practice at home, away from the cameras and the scoring, is the better route.

Palmer, who has been close to Woods for years and has often offered him advice, said that he was not worried that the younger man would let the decision linger.

"He's a competitor. He's going to figure out how to get ready," Palmer said. "He always has."

The absence will be felt in Orlando. Woods is one of the biggest draws in the sport, and his presence at Bay Hill has long meant bigger galleries, higher television ratings and extra buzz around the property. Tournament officials had hoped to see him at least take a look at the course before moving on to Augusta, but they have said they respect that the decision belongs to Woods.

Palmer's reaction is typical of a man who has spent decades treating other golfers with generosity. He has been a mentor to several generations of players, and he has frequently said that the game is bigger than any one tournament or any one name.

Still, he made it clear that he hopes to see Woods back on the course soon, and in better form.

"The Masters is a special place for him, and for all of us," Palmer said. "I hope he gets it going. Golf needs Tiger playing well."

For now, the focus shifts to the rest of the field at Bay Hill, where the contenders will try to claim a victory in Palmer's honor. Woods, meanwhile, will continue his preparations in private, with one goal in sight: arriving at Augusta in shape to compete.

Whether that work will pay off remains to be seen. What is clear is that the sport will be watching closely, and that its elder statesman is firmly in his corner.

The use of animals in scientific research is one of the most debated ethical questions in modern science. On one side, animal studies have contributed to major medical advances, including vaccines, insulin, and organ transplantation. Without them, many diseases that are now treatable might still be fatal. Researchers argue that when the goal is saving human lives, limited animal testing is justified.

On the other side, animals are capable of pain and fear, and critics argue that causing suffering for human benefit is morally difficult to defend. Moreover, animal models do not always predict human outcomes, which weakens some of the claimed benefits.

In my view, animal research can be ethical only under strict conditions. It should be used when no alternative exists, kept to the minimum necessary, and designed to reduce suffering. The "three Rs" of replacement, reduction, and refinement offer a practical guide. As technologies such as organ-on-a-chip systems and computer modeling improve, we should work toward a future where animal testing is rare. Until then, careful regulation and transparency are essential.

Because our tastes evolved for a world where calories were scarce. Fat, sugar and salt were rare and valuable, so humans developed strong cravings for them, and our brains reward us with dopamine when we eat them. Modern food companies exploit this by engineering products with just the right mix of those ingredients, often cheaply and in huge quantities. Healthy foods like vegetables are usually lower in calories and flavor intensity, so they trigger less of a reward. There's also a bias in how we judge it: many "best tasting" foods are treats we eat for pleasure rather than nutrition, so we notice their downsides more. Plenty of delicious foods, like ripe fruit, grilled fish or fresh bread with olive oil, are perfectly healthy.

The Earth's rotation does not directly change flight duration in a meaningful way, because the atmosphere rotates along with the planet. An aircraft therefore moves relative to the air around it, not relative to the ground below. Consequently, a plane does not gain or lose time simply because the surface is turning beneath it.

However, rotation indirectly influences travel times through wind patterns. Prevailing westerly winds, including the jet stream, are shaped partly by the Earth's rotation. Flights traveling eastward, such as from New York to London, often benefit from tailwinds and arrive sooner, while westbound flights face headwinds and take longer. Rotation also creates minor effects such as the Coriolis force, but these are accounted for in navigation and are negligible for duration.

**Handwritten "American Pie" Lyrics Sell for $1.2 Million at Auction**

NEW YORK -- The original handwritten lyrics to Don McLean's "American Pie" have sold at auction for $1.2 million, a price that underscores the enduring pull of one of the best-known songs in American music.

The manuscript, which includes drafts, notes and revisions, offers a rare look at how the singer-songwriter shaped the eight-and-a-half-minute ballad. The song was released in 1971 and reached No. 1 in 1972, and it remains McLean's biggest hit.

Few pop songs have inspired as much debate. Its verses are crowded with symbolism, from a jester and a king to a "day the music died," widely understood to refer to the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson. For decades, fans and critics have argued over what the rest of the imagery means.

McLean has long declined to offer a full explanation. But he has said the lyrics and notes being sold will reveal the song's meaning to whoever studies them closely.

"Basically, they will see what it's about," he has said of the material, though he has stopped short of spelling it out himself.

Auction officials said interest in the lot was strong, with several bidders competing for the manuscript. They described it as a significant piece of music and cultural history, given the song's popularity across generations and its place in the national memory.

Scholars of popular music say the sale reflects a growing market for artifacts tied to well-known songwriters. Handwritten lyric sheets, they note, can show a creative process that finished recordings conceal, including lines that were crossed out, rewritten or abandoned.

The identity of the buyer was not disclosed. Whether the new owner will share the manuscript with the public, or help settle the long-running puzzle of the song's meaning, remains to be seen.

Before typewriters became common in the late nineteenth century, applying for a job looked quite different from what we know today. There was no standard résumé, and the process depended heavily on personal connections, reputation, and handwritten communication.

## How people heard about openings

**Word of mouth and social networks.** Most jobs were filled through family, neighbors, church members, and tradespeople. A farmer might hear from a friend that a blacksmith needed a helper, or a merchant might ask his relatives whether anyone knew a capable clerk. Reputation mattered enormously, because in small communities everyone's character and work habits were widely known.

**Apprenticeships and guilds.** For skilled trades, the usual route was an apprenticeship. Parents or guardians often arranged the position directly with a master craftsman, sometimes paying a fee. Guilds in European towns controlled who could enter a trade, so hearing about openings meant being connected to the guild system.

**Public notices.** In towns and cities, employers posted handbills or notices on doors, in marketplaces, and at inns. Newspapers, which spread widely during the 1700s, carried advertisements. Colonial American papers, for example, ran notices seeking servants, tutors, clerks, and laborers. Hiring fairs, held in parts of England and elsewhere, let workers and employers meet in a public place. Laborers would stand in the town square, sometimes carrying a tool or symbol of their trade, to show what work they could do.

## How people applied

**Letters of introduction and recommendation.** For clerical, professional, or household positions, applicants often relied on a letter of recommendation from a respected person such as a minister, a former employer, or a local official. This letter functioned like a modern reference, and sometimes carried more weight than the applicant's own words.

**Handwritten letters of application.** Educated applicants wrote letters by hand, often in a formal and polite style, describing their qualifications and asking for consideration. Penmanship counted. A clerk's job depended on neat, legible writing, so the letter itself served as a work sample.

**In-person visits.** For many trades and manual jobs, the "application" was simply showing up. A person would go to a workshop, farm, or shop, speak with the owner, and perhaps demonstrate their skills on the spot.

## Why it worked this way

Without mass communication and with limited literacy in many places, trust was the main currency. Employers wanted someone they could vouch for, which made patronage and personal connection more important than formal credentials. Written records existed, but they supported relationships instead of replacing them.

For your assignment, it may help to compare this with modern hiring, where résumés and online postings are standard, to highlight how technology changed the process.
